item.title: Cybercrims go beyond stealing data to attack physical building systems
item.description:
Late Sunday night, a still-unknown cybercriminal or group hacked thousands of remote-controlled refrigeration systems across hundreds of French grocery stores , spiking temperatures, spoiling food, and sparking fires. This is part of an ongoing trend of attacking physical systems that can do damage in the real world.

In August, a ransomware attack disrupted building-management systems at a Canadian hospital, affecting door access controls, central HVAC monitoring, and the issuing of staff access cards.

And three years ago, cyberattacks hit Las Vegas casinos , causing slot machines to go dark, preventing payment kiosks and ATMs from spitting out cash, and locking guests out of their rooms when the electronic keys stopped working.

Not all digital intrusions remain in cyberspace, and attackers don’t need to encrypt files and steal data to cause chaos. Hitting physical systems often produces more severe consequences - and turns up the heat on executives to pay an extortion demand.

“There was one gig where the customer was refusing to pay, and so the threat actor was like, ‘Hold my beer, have fun getting into your offices,’ and locked everybody out,” Tim Beasley, a senior incident response consultant at Semperis, told The Register .

Beasley won’t name the customer, or provide any incriminating information, but said the incident response involved police smashing glass in addition to his team recovering compromised data.

“The cops had to break in, and literally get into the building, breaking some windows, so the customer was able to finally get back in,” he said. We asked if the customer paid the ransom demand, and Beasley yelled: “Oh, hell, no!”

A report published earlier this month by ServiceNow’s Armis Labs found increasing evidence of ransomware attackers using physical consequences as leverage in their intrusions. “Today’s BAS operate at the intersection of IT and OT worlds, creating unprecedented exposure,” the report said .

Ransomware with physical consequences

Building automation systems - BAS - are the critical systems that control and monitor facilities’ HVAC, lighting, energy usage, and water consumption. They also oversee badge readers, door locks, surveillance cameras, fire alarm control panels, and other physical safety equipment.

As such, BAS make very attractive targets for ransomware operators looking for high-pressure ways to extort organizations into paying multi-million ransom demands. These systems also appeal to government-backed goons and hacktivists looking to ensure maximum psychological and physical impact during destructive cyberattacks.

Armis Labs found 73 percent of organizations own BAS that have been used in ransomware attacks, and this same percentage have known exploited vulnerabilities in at least one of their building automation systems. Additionally, 91 percent of BAS communicate over insecure protocols - opening up an even bigger attack surface for cyber-miscreants wanting to cause physical harm.

“The primary thing that we see with any attack on building management systems or physical systems: It’s a great place for the threat actor to hide,” Michael Freeman, ServiceNow’s senior director of threat research, told The Register . “It's easier for them to compromise, and it's easier for them to hide in.”

BAS and operational technology (OT) in general have fewer security controls than IT systems. Most require continual uptime, which makes them harder to patch or even scan for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations as this may lead to outages.

“One case in particular, against a very large financial institution, the threat actors were staying low and quiet by attacking their BMS systems, and then pivoting into the IT environment,” Freeman said.

The intruders were routinely caught - and booted from - the financial institution’s IT systems, so they built backdoors into the BMS to ensure persistent access to both OT and IT networks.

“We're also seeing threat actors using AI to understand more building automation systems, especially ones that are using obscure OSs like VxWorks, older Unix-type systems,” Freeman said.

AI has entered the chat

As multiple security experts have told us in previous interviews, security through obscurity is dead . Not only does AI make it easier for attackers to find bugs – some very obscure and decades old - but it also means criminals no longer need to be OT experts to carry out destructive cyberattacks on critical networks and facilities. Instead, they can use AI to learn all about the obscure protocols and proprietary hardware and software that historically made industrial control systems black boxes.

“It’s easier to understand what the controls are,” Freeman said, using the example of an attacker trying to take down a plane, or some similar catastrophic cyberattack.

Historically, even advanced, government-backed hacking squads would “be quiet, because you don't know what changing certain settings is going to do,” Freeman explained. “Now you can use AI to say, ‘If I compromise a weight and balance system for airlines, all I need to do now is move this number here to this number, and I just told the system to load heavy stuff on the right side of the plane instead of equal distribution.'”

Freeman told us he has seen attackers break into airlines’ OT gear in the past. “But they didn’t know what they were getting into, and so they left them alone,” he said. “Those do cause me concern because in the past I've helped to kick people out of those types of systems.”

Industrial orgs increasingly under attack

OT security provider Dragos tracks ransomware groups’ claims against industrial organizations on the criminals’ leak sites, along with publicly disclosed intrusions affecting manufacturing and other critical sectors. To be clear: claims on leak sites aren’t always accurate or even true, and the claim itself doesn’t mean operations or control systems were hit.

Since 2022, however, “the numbers have been consistently increasing,” Lexie Mooney, senior threat analyst at Dragos, told The Register .

The cybersecurity firm tracked 995 ransomware attacks against industrial orgs in 2023, a 49.5 percent increase from 2022. That number j umped more than 87 percent in 2024 .

Active ransomware groups targeting industrial orgs also grew in 2024 to 80 groups, up from 50 the year before.

Dragos tracked 119 ransomware groups impacting more than 3,300 industrial organizations in 2025, and the incidents have steadily increased every quarter this year: 1,020 incidents in the first quarter of 2026 and 1,140 incidents in Q2 .

“The vast majority of cases are opportunistic,” Abdul Alamri, a senior threat analyst at Dragos, told us. “In some of the cases that we have seen an operational impact, either physical systems or an OT operation, it’s just the nature of the opportunism on the part of those ransomware groups.”

This is partially due to the complexity of OT systems, he added. “Ransomware groups want to disrupt operations, and put pressure on the victims to pay the ransom,” Alamri said. “They don’t want to invest that time and effort to target complex systems."

It’s usually quicker and easier for financially motivated crims to affect operations via IT systems - as the extortionists did in the August 2025 Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) breach , which halted manufacturing and crippled business operations for months.

Internet-connected OT: the next 'low-hanging fruit'

The other side of this complexity, however, is that many organizations themselves still lack visibility into their OT environments.

Dragos estimates that fewer than 10 percent of OT networks worldwide currently have sufficient network monitoring in place. Plus, in 30 percent of incidents the security firm responded to in 2025, the investigations did not begin with a detection alert, but with someone noticing that “something seemed wrong” in operations.

This lack of visibility, combined with threats from AI , worries Alamri. “If you compare the risk that we have seen from humans, to what we are about to face in the near future with AI agents who might continuously try to break into those systems - it’s a pretty dark future if we don't take the right measures to protect ourselves against it.”

As organizations get better at patching and securing IT systems, attackers will likely look to internet-connected OT systems where digital compromises have real-world consequences, according to Matt Hayden, VP of cyber and emerging threats at General Dynamics Information Technology.

“We all anticipate that as we get better at reducing the IT low-hanging fruit, OT will become a vector of much more scrutiny and much more attention,” Hayden told The Register .

Before joining GDIT, Hayden served as the assistant secretary for cyber, infrastructure, risk and resilience policy at the US Department of Homeland Security.

Compliance vs. security

“There is a big focus on the hardware being connected for the purpose of compliance - and to make sure that, in the name of compliance, we aren't opening back doors, to devices that traditionally wouldn't have to be connected to facilitate their service,” he said, using refrigeration units as an example of one such system that is now internet-connected for compliance purposes.

This was prior to the French supermarket hacks.

Refrigeration units’ monitoring systems connect to the internet so their owners and operators can prove to regulators that the units maintain their uptime and temperature in accordance with regulations.

“So if the health department comes by, they say, ‘Look, my refrigerator was at 27 degrees for the last 72 days,' and they have a check mark, and they get their A plus. But that simple connectivity is also a vector in which that particular refrigerant unit could be targeted for disruption,” Hayden said.

About a week after our interview, criminals did exactly that.

“The recently reported exploitations of commercial refrigeration units represent a significant example of devices without digital value, no sensitive data or extended enterprise access, being exploited by being connected to the internet with unpatched firmware,” Hayden told us in a subsequent email.

He said he expects the attribution to be “less nation-state, and more likely those looking for targets of opportunity to identify what could be done with the unpatched systems.”

“The consequences are food supply degradation at a small scale, but it is an important example of what could happen at scale very quickly with more consequential operating equipment,” Hayden said.®

item.title: Amazon wants you to Bee-lieve wearable AI can recall it all for you
item.description:
Amazon wants to ensure you have a personal AI that you can carry with you anywhere, listening in on your conversations so it can remind you of key details – and give you personalized shopping recommendations, of course.

The global online bazaar has unveiled two new AI-based products from Bee, a startup in wearable devices that it acquired last year in a deal said to be worth $300 million.

Bee’s original product for Amazon was tried out and sort of given approval by friend of The Register Corey Quinn, Chief Cloud Economist at Duckbill, earlier this year.

One new gizmo, Bee Frontier , is designed to be worn like a watch or one of those fitness trackers, although to our mind it looks more like you are wearing a doorbell.

The other, Bee Eclipse , is a slimline and lightweight device about the size of a credit card that attaches to the back of your phone magnetically, like a limpet.

Both are intended to listen in to your conversations and help you remember important details, like when you are meeting your friend for a pint later and at which hospitality outlet. The devices take note of the details you might otherwise forget, and then turn them into useful conversation summaries, to-dos and reminders, Amazon says.

The pair of devices feature a single button to turn on or off, and a visible indicator that lights up when one is listening in and its AI is summarizing the conversation.

When enabled, the eavesdropper gathers context from your conversations to provide insights and recommendations. Summaries of your conversations can be accessed via a Bee mobile app on iPhone or Android (linked via Bluetooth), or an all-new desktop app. These can be organized using templates for things such as lectures, or users can just review memories from the past few days to see what you discussed.

The Bee devices pick up on trends or themes that recur, and recommend personalized goals and actions. That sounds alarm bells for us, as it suggests the AI is designed to get to know you, and what you like.

Along with the new hardware, Bee has now gained the ability to connect to Amazon’s Alexa+ AI assistant and Amazon.com, which means that you can ask Alexa for a meeting summary - or get personalized shopping recommendations from Amazon based on what your personal earwig has gleaned.

However, Amazon says that the latest Bee products respect user privacy, as audio is processed into insights in real time and not stored, while transcripts are encrypted and only the user can access them.

Bee Frontier is claimed to have IP67 water resistance, up to seven days of battery life, and has a USB-C charging port. Bee Eclipse also has a USB-C port but is said to last for more than 21 days of use from a single battery charge.

Both devices come in a choice of colors, with Bee Frontier available now for $74.99 and Bee Eclipse due to be available shortly for $99.99. ®

item.title: Get in the bin! UK Space Agency wants public to name its debris removal mission
item.description:
The UK Space Agency needs a name for its Active Debris Removal Mission and has decided that the great British public are the people for the job.

The agency confirmed the operation earlier this week and selected ClearSpace UK to lead it. The plan is to remove two UK-registered satellites from Low Earth Orbit, with the clean-up due to begin in 2029.

The UK government is backing the effort with more than £60 million, and it expects the disposal to be completed by 2032.

The spacecraft will grab each satellite, drop it into a lower orbit for disposal by burning up in the Earth's atmosphe, then climb to a higher one to await its next job. Less suicide dive, more cosmic bin round. And because it’s refuellable, the UK government says it "can help make a difference and sweep space for years to come."

Launch is planned from SaxaVord Spaceport in Scotland.

But first, the quest needs a name . The Active Debris Removal Mission hardly trips off the tongue, and the UK Space Agency gave inspirational examples of other project names, such as NASA's Mercury program (named after the Roman god) or Tim Peake's Principia mission (inspired by Sir Isaac Newton's Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica).

Oddly, the agency didn't mention the poll to brand a scientific research ship, which was eventually named Sir David Attenborough rather than Boaty McBoatface, the most popular suggestion .

The tag must consist of two words – so no "Itsy bitsy teeny weeny orbit debris clear machiney" – and 150 words to explain the name and how it reflects the theme. So no backronyms, for example Broom ( B ritish R obotic O rbital O bject M anipulator). Starry McBinface?

Obviously, swear words are not allowed, nor is anything deemed "potentially offensive" or political. Using anything that might attract copyright or intellectual property lawyers is also out.

Letting the public suggest a name feels potentially riskier than the mission itself, though it should generate some engagement. It's a high-risk, high-reward campaign; there are plenty of dead satellites cluttering orbit, and the ability to remove them is becoming increasingly important.

Rob Atchison, Managing Director of ClearSpace UK, said, "Our next step is to design, build and test a spacecraft that can get close, safely, to an object never designed to be caught, and take control of it."

If you're getting a sense of déjà vu about this expedition, you're probably right. The European Space Agency (ESA) announced ClearSpace-1 in 2019, which the agency called "the first space mission to remove an item of debris from orbit" with a launch set for 2025. At the time, ClearSpace founder and CEO Luc Piguet said: "This is the right time for such a mission."

In latest announcement, Piguet called the UKSA's selection "an important milestone."

This is far from the first mission to grapple an object in orbit. Most recently, Katalyst Space sent its LINK spacecraft to rescue NASA's Swift observatory. That was intended to capture the Swift spacecraft and raise its altitude, but failures with LINK doomed it .

Perhaps things might have gone better if the public had been given an opportunity to name the spacecraft? ®

item.title: Open-weight models win hearts, minds, and wallets
item.description:
Open-weight models more than quadrupled their share of spending through Vercel's AI Gateway between June and September, when they processed more than seven in 10 tokens.

"In August, open-weight models processed the majority of AI Gateway token volume for the first time," the biz said . "The money is now following. Open weight's share of spend has more than quadrupled over the last three months, from one in twenty gateway dollars in June to nearly one in four in September."

AI Gateway, like OpenRouter, acts as an intermediary that allows customers to purchase tokens from different AI providers through a common interface. While it works with popular harnesses like Claude Code and Codex and provides access to proprietary and open-weight models, it doesn't see usage through other gateways or from customers who access AI models directly from vendors or through on-premises hosting.

While gateway spending in September was about 13x higher than recorded in December 2025, the average price per token was about 47 percent lower, according to Vercel. At the same time, almost one in three teams changed their most-used AI provider in September, suggesting that market competition may be limiting vendor lock-in.

The most popular model in September was TypeSafe AI's Jev . In just 14 days, it reached 35 percent of paid teams using Vercel's AI Gateway, the company said. Its popularity didn't generate much spending due to the model's architecture – usage accounted for only 1 percent of the month’s tokens and 0.15 percent of spending.

US-based models from Anthropic and OpenAI still attract the largest portion of spending in September, with 11.03 percent going to Claude Opus 5.5, followed by GPT-6 Astra at 4.86 percent. But models from Chinese AI providers have become more popular. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ranked third in spending, at 4.19 percent.

More than two-thirds of the September spending on Chinese models went to US providers serving those models, up from less than a tenth in December 2025, Vercel said.

Moonshot AI, maker of Kimi, captured 3.6 percent of gateway tokens and 13.2 percent of spend in September; DeepSeek took 58 percent of tokens for just 6.6 percent of spend; and Z.ai, maker of GLM-5.3, took 7.2 percent of tokens and 4.5 percent of spend.

So efforts to ban or limit open-weight models, something considered by the current US administration, would affect American businesses serving those models and their customers.

Even if the US continues to dither on AI policy, trade barriers affecting AI models may alter market dynamics. China on Friday proposed adding 40 technology items to its export control list , 23 of them related to AI. The Associated Press notes that Moonshot’s Kimi K3 and Alibaba’s Qwen 3.8-Max are among the models that meet the parameter threshold set by Chinese authorities, though the official message did not identify affected models.

"This introduces significant uncertainty for US businesses that host or rely on Chinese models," Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said in a social media post.

"Particularly given that Chinese AI labs are moving toward licensing the use of open-source models to generate revenue, the Chinese government stating that it has the ability to curtail those licensing agreements at any time should make US businesses more hesitant to rely on those models going forward."

McGuire said the US needs to adopt a comprehensive regulatory framework governing the use of US AI technology overseas and include Chinese AI models used or hosted in the United States in its domestic AI regulations.®

item.title: Benchmarked: Nvidia's RTX Spark notebook delivers serious local AI compute, at a price
item.description:
Nvidia's RTX Spark partner systems are here, and spec-for-spec they've got all the ingredients for a hit: a potent CPU, blisteringly fast integrated graphics, and up to 128 GB of unified memory in a lightweight, ultra-premium package that's ready to run demanding models locally.

But with prices for these systems starting around $2,600 and going well north of $6,000 for the top spec trims, the one thing RTX Spark isn't is a good deal.

However, for the right person, by which we mostly mean AI enthusiasts, researchers, and/or creative professionals who need tons of video memory and don't want to get lost in Apple's walled garden or would prefer Nvidia's CUDA ecosystem over AMD's ROCm, the RTX Spark still has a lot to offer.

As such, we'll be largely focusing on the local agentic AI use cases Nvidia and Microsoft are pushing for these "builder-class" systems.

The Register had the opportunity this week to put the OmniBook Ultra, HP's unique spin on the RTX Spark platform, through a series of AI benchmarks to see just how well it performs. And spoiler alert: you'll be hard pressed to find a faster Windows notebook for local AI.

But before diving into performance, let's take a closer look at the hardware itself.

No-compromise quality

Lifting the lid on the OmniBook Ultra 16, the first thing you'll notice is the gorgeous 2880x1800 pixel OLED touchscreen with a 16:10 aspect ratio.

Touch screens on professional notebooks can be a contentious topic. You either love them or hate them, but at the end of the day, if the idea of fingerprints obscuring your work gives you pause, no one is forcing you to use it, and we're happy to see it here.

The OmniBook Ultra's display is mounted to a surprisingly stiff hinge mechanism mounted to the top of the chassis. This has the benefit of keeping the hinge out of the way of the notebook's ample exhaust, which is kind of important because the 20-core N1X system-on-chip powering our review unit runs hot.

The system's ample venting keeps most of that heat concentrated around the base of the display and for the most part, away from the keyboard.

Speaking of keyboards, the OmniBook Ultra's digit fidgets are a bit of a throwback. Instead of the now-ubiquitous chiclet keys popularized by Apple in the early '10s, HP has gone for a more traditional notebook keyboard, which we found refreshingly easy to type on.

Keyboards of course are subjective so if there's any question on whether this one is right for you, it might be worth a trip to your local big box store to give one a good pecking before you commit.

Framing the keyboard are a pair of speaker grilles backed by four Cirrus Logic amplifiers which sound excellent for a Windows notebook, but can't quite match the clarity and bass of Apple's MacBook Pros.

With that said, we don't expect anyone will be disappointed by the OmniBook Ultra's speakers. Directly below the keyboard is a haptic trackpad that is as precise as it is enormous. No product in this price class should be shipping with a diving board mechanism in 2026, so it's nice to see HP didn't cheap out on us.

Moving to the sides of the notebook, you'll find a refreshingly comprehensive set of ports including:

  • 3.5mm headphone microphone combo port.

  • 2x USB-4 Type C ports (40 Gbps)

  • HDMI

  • 2x USB-A (10 Gbps).

  • MicroSD

Our only real critique here is that the OmniBook Ultra, like other laptops, lacks a full size SD card slot. MicroSD cards are convenient, but they're not widely used in professional environments and we'd have preferred to see a full size SD card reader or better yet a CFexpress card reader. However, it's rare if not impossible to see these on notebooks.

The chassis itself weighs in at 4.89 pounds and is milled from aluminum with a remarkably premium-feeling finish on the palm rest, lid, and bottom panels. HP has done a nice job building a notebook that feels as premium as it is powerful.

Into the belly of the beast

While the OmniBook Ultra is an objectively nice machine, the main attraction of any of the RTX Spark systems is going to be the N1X chip powering them.

The SoC features a MediaTek-derived CPU chiplet that's melded using advanced packaging and Nvidia's NVLink Fusion chip-to-chip interconnect to a Blackwell GPU.

The N1X comes in two flavors: An entry level version with 18 CPU cores and a GPU with 5,120 CUDAs. Meanwhile, the highest-end SKU — the one found in our review unit — features up to 20 CPU cores and a GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores. If you're wondering, that's exactly the same number as found in Nvidia's RTX 5070 just with access to a whole lot more memory.

We'll note that not all of those CPU cores are created equal. Like most Arm-based SoCs, the N1X contains a mix of big and little cores. Specifically, it has an equal complement of Arm X925 and Cortex A725 cores.

While all of this sounds impressive, it's worth noting that the chip really isn't all that new. The N1X is based heavily on the GB10, which launched in the Linux-based DGX Spark over a year ago. With that said, there have been some improvements.

At Hot Chips 2025, we learned the GB10 would support memory up to 9,400 MT/s. But, when the DGX Spark finally arrived that fall, it was only sporting 8,533 MT/s memory. The N1X rectifies this by boosting memory bandwidth to around 300 GB/s.

Higher memory bandwidth usually translates to faster token generation in AI inference and agentic workloads. So, while a fairly modest boost in bandwidth over the DGX Spark's 273 GB/s, it's still a meaningful one.

And that brings us to performance.

Your own personal AI assistant

There aren't many modern workloads that really need 128 GB of unified memory, but local AI certainly is one of them. While you can certainly get away with less, it opens the door to models with a decent shot at replacing something like Claude Code or Codex.

In fact, Microsoft believes that the future of Windows will be that of Copilot+ PCs that can run a mix of local and remote models with prompts routed between them based on things like complexity or privacy. Redmond is calling this technique hybrid intelligence.

But even with 128 GB of shared memory on board, you're still somewhat limited on what models can actually fit. That's because, unlike on Linux, which allocates memory dynamically to the DGX Spark's GPU as needed, Windows isn't quite asur testi smart.

The HP OmniBook Ultra arrived with a 50:50 split with 64 GB dedicated to the CPU and GPU respectively. This can be reconfigured as needed, but it's not exactly ideal. The good news is that, with the right software, you can get around this. Llama.cpp, one of the most popular local LLM inference frameworks, allows for overflowing into CPU memory as needed and, since the CPU and GPU share the same memory, the performance penalty isn't nearly as stark as it would when using a dedicated GPU.

Having said that, you have to fit a lot more than just the model's weights into memory. For agentic AI harnesses like Claude Code, models need to support large context windows with 128,000 tokens being a sweet spot these days. Depending on the model, that can chew up an awful lot of memory.

There is also the issue of the available models. While you could theoretically cram a 200 billion parameter model onto an RTX Spark using Llama.cpp, there aren't really many models that size.

Batch 1 performance

Since Nvidia's RTX Spark platform ships with Windows, we conducted all of our tests using the v0.6.0 build of Llama.cpp across five models developed by Meta, Google, and Alibaba in sizes ranging from around 26 to 122 billion parameters.

Our first test simulates a chatbot-like environment tasking each system and model to process and generate a 256 token input and output.

There are two metrics worth paying attention to here: Time to first token (TTFT) measures the time in milliseconds required for the GPU to process the prompt and generally reflects the GPU's compute performance. Tokens per second (Tok/s) is a little more obvious and reflects how quickly the system can churn out tokens once the prompt has been processed. Also called decode, token generation is usually dependent on memory bandwidth, so faster memory tends to perform better here.

Across our test suite, we see performance scales neatly with model size and active parameter count.

Pitted against AMD's Strix Halo and Nvidia's earlier DGX Spark systems, which, again, aren't ideal comparison points since they're mini PCs with more robust cooling systems, the HP OmniBook Ultra performs quite well.

In Qwen3.6-35B-A3B — the fastest model we tested on any of the systems — the N1X's faster memory did give it an edge over the DGX Spark in token generation. The GB10 does appear to offer slightly higher compute performance, perhaps due to better thermals. Both Nvidia-based systems offer better performance than AMD's Strix Halo platform in our tests, though this shouldn't come as a surprise. On paper, Strix Halo offers less performance and memory bandwidth than either Nvidia chip and we've repeatedly shown this in testing over the past year. AMD's saving grace is that it has consistently offered better value.

Local AI agents

While our single batch and context scaling benchmarks are useful for quantifying system performance across models, they aren't necessarily representative of how you're likely to use local models today.

If our numbers seem a little low compared to other benchmarks for the N1X and GB10, that's because our single batch results don't take advantage of prefill caching or speculative decoding.

If you're not familiar, prefill caching helps to speed up prompt processing time for information the model has already seen before. Speculative decoding meanwhile involves using a small draft model to predict the outputs of a larger one. In highly repetitive workloads, like agentic coding, speculative decoding speeds up token generation by 2-3x without any loss in quality.

AI agents, like code assistants, pass over the same prompts, code bases, and resources recursively, which makes them prime candidates for both techniques. In real world benchmarks, the overall line up remains unchanged to see high overall performance from these systems.

This test measures system performance when running an agentic coding workflow using Alibaba's Qwen Code (not to be confused with the Qwen-Coder family of models) harness and measures how quickly each system and model can solve a bin packing problem.

This addresses one of the more interesting phenomena that has cropped up around agentic AI. Faster token generation doesn't necessarily translate to a faster time to solve. Smarter but slower models can still be faster if they use fewer tokens to arrive at the correct answer.

And we see that here. Large models like Qwen3.5-122B-A10B ran slower on our test systems, generating tokens at roughly half the rate of the smaller 35B parameter model. Yet, the median time to solve was roughly 40 seconds faster on the larger model because it needed only a fraction of the tokens.

Having said that, given the extreme cost of memory right now, we believe the sweet spot for local AI code assistants is somewhere in the 20-60 billion parameter range, which is small enough to run on less expensive 64 GB versions of Nvidia's RTX Spark systems.

Teething troubles

As you might expect, any new platform is going to have a few growing pains at launch. It was certainly true when Intel introduced its performance and efficiency cores and when Qualcomm brought its Arm-based Snapdragon X Elite SoCs to the PC. Nvidia's RTX Spark platform is no different.

During our testing, we observed issues with thermal throttling or rather an apparent lack thereof. Under a constant AI inference load, we experienced occasional lock ups and, on one occasion, graphical artifacts as the GPU exceeded 90 degrees Celsius.

AI inference and training are some of the most resource-intensive workloads ever developed and to call them resource viruses wouldn't be inaccurate. So it's not surprising that a sustained inference load over the course of several hours might overwhelm the thin-and-light's thermal management system.

Under real world conditions we don't expect this will be an issue. Even a few seconds between prompts was enough for the notebook to remain stable and artifact free. With that said, if you were hoping to fine tune LLMs, you might want to look at Nvidia's DGX Spark or any one of the other GB10-based AI workstations from HP, Dell, Lenovo, and others. Their larger chassis and thermal management systems make them far better candidates for the often hours-long process of fine tuning models. Software support for PyTorch also happens to be a bit better on Linux than on Windows.

Beyond a cooling system that's perhaps a bit optimistic for what is supposed to be a 140 watt SoC, the only glitch we ran into was the Cirrus Logic audio outputs disabling themselves out of the blue. Thankfully all it took to get them running again was to uninstall them in device manager and reboot.

Summing up

The OmniBook Ultra 16 and the rest of the RTX Spark lineup occupy a rather niche segment in 2026. With memory prices at an all time high, the system spans the gamut from ultra-premium thin-and-light in its base config and mobile workstation at the upper end of the spectrum.

The OmniBook Ultra 16 is an objectively strong performer and an extremely well built one at that.

But at around $3,200 for the base model OmniBook Ultra 16 with the N1X and $6,229 as tested here, none of these systems are cheap. Had Nvidia and its partners launched these notebooks a year ago at between $2,000 and $4,000, the story might have been different.

Unless you've drunk the AI Kool-Aid and are buying an RTX Spark system for local AI development or happen to have a particularly VRAM hungry workload that makes you money, these systems are going to be a tough sell for the same reason it's hard to recommend workstation components to the average consumer. Most folks can't take full advantage of them and their money is usually better spent elsewhere. And if you can and you're willing to give up a little performance, AMD's Strix and Gorgon Halo-based notebooks and mini PCs are definitely worth cross shopping.

As memory prices normalize, we do expect Nvidia's next-generation of RTX Spark systems to be both faster and more attractively priced. Unfortunately, we will wait a while for that to happen. The memory fabs expect DRAM supplies to remain constrained through at least 2028.

We've got a whole lot more testing planned for the RTX Spark and HP's OmniBook Ultra, including a comprehensive set of CPU and gaming benchmarks, along with a deeper dive into agentic AI performance as we look to answer the question whether these systems can actually save you money. So far that argument isn't looking good. ®

item.title: Node.js creator ditches Deno to work on open source Cloudflare Workers
item.description:
Node.js creator Ryan Dahl is sacrificing a battle to win the war … for server-side computing and allowing Node-replacement Deno to fall by the wayside.

Last week, Cloudflare announced that it had purchased Dahl’s company Deno, which was built around an open source server-side JavaScript runtime of the same name that he created, to compete with the Node.js runtime, which he also created. Nonetheless, Deno has no future at Cloudflare, which will maintain the runtime for another year before ending its development.

That’s OK with Dahl.

"I am now of the opinion that if you're choosing Node.js for building servers, you’re doing it wrong," Dahl told The Register .

For Cloudflare, the Deno buy is an acquihire for Dahl and 12 of his Deno colleagues, who will work to build out Cloudflare’s Workers platform, expanding it for potential open-source use. He feels this approach is the way to go.

“Right now, every other server is really operating at the Linux VM layer. That is not what Cloudflare Workers are," he said.

The unstoppable force of Node.js

Dahl’s Node.js, which he presented to the world in 2009, sparked a revolution in Web application architecture. He was fed up with the Apache web server hogging all the memory.  Using the Google V8 JavaScript engine, Node not only could execute JavaScript code on the server, but it could concurrently serve thousands of requests per second with a fraction of the memory required by the traditional choice of the time, Apache Web server. Today, Node powers about 30 million websites worldwide. With 130 million downloads, it probably runs a lot more internal operations as well.

The ever-fickle Dahl first debuted Deno in 2018 as a rewrite of Node. The name ‘Deno’ is an anagram of Node, and it was Dahl’s attempt to fix everything he felt he got wrong with Node – built-in fetch, a permission model, native TypeScript support et al.

Sequoia backed Dahl’s company for $21 million in 2022, and as of August, Deno amassed 400,000 monthly users. Nonetheless, Node’s gravity proved too heavy for Deno to achieve escape velocity.

“What we found over years of working on Deno is that you can't really deviate from Node.js very much," Dahl told The Register . "As we continued to try to get adoption for Deno, we found we had to essentially backpedal on some of the original promises and become more Node compatible over time, and that left us as a kind of an alternative Node.js implementation.”

Going forward, Cloudflare will supply Deno with bug fixes and security patches for the next year, while Dahl looks for a new home for the MIT-licensed open source project (the OpenJS Foundation perhaps?).

The new way: distributed micro-servers

In August, Dahl released an entirely new project , called celld, which was an open source implementation of Cloudflare’s Durable Objects. He was fascinated by the technology, originally created by Kenton Varda .

“A primitive this good deserves to run anywhere,” the celld page stated.

Durable Objects allow developers to build stateful, real-time distributed applications. Unlike Node or Deno, the resulting application doesn’t require a dedicated runtime environment. It runs on Cloudflare’s serverless Workers runtime , which executes code inside Google JavaScript V8 isolates — a lightweight sandbox running within a single OS process.

Individual instances of the application can be spun up at an edge location closest to the user. Each Durable Object instance acts as a single-threaded micro-server with a unique global ID and its own co-located storage, where user data for the session is stored in its own dedicated copy of SQLite.

Durable Objects “is kind of the perfect distributed systems abstraction,” Dahl said.

The drawback of Durable Objects for Dahl was that it was hard-wired into Cloudflare’s infrastructure. He created celld as an implementation that could be hosted anywhere, not just on Cloudflare.

As it turns out, Cloudflare had similar aspirations. In 2022, the company had open-sourced a version of the Workers runtime, called workerd, but the release was more geared towards developer testing. The company never got around to making Workers fully self hosting, much less giving it the chops to maintain distributed state, a power Dahl gave to celld.

So the mission for Dahl's team is to merge the work of celld with workerd for a stand-alone JavaScript/WebAssembly runtime, while integrating it with Workers and Durable Objects as much as possible. (celld is also going bye-bye.)

Such a technology could be yet another revolutionary turn for server-side JavaScript, offering a runtime that would require only 300 KB of memory per instance, rather than the hundreds of megabytes now required for Node/Deno. Such savings could quickly add up for a cloud provider, especially one serving the voracious agentic market.

But until we see the fruits of Dahl’s team, the market for independent runtimes will be squeezed, what with the absence of Deno and Anthropic’s recent acquisition ( and rewriting ) of Bun. Now, Dahl’s first creation, the mighty Node, will have to go it alone.®

item.title: Meta grants itself right to scrape content from business customers for model training
item.description:
Businesses using Facebook commercially may want to think twice about what information they share online. At the end of the month, Meta plans to introduce terms that would authorize it to collect content from websites associated with its business customers and use it to train AI models or otherwise improve its products.

The ad biz has revised its commercial terms of service, and the new contractual language takes effect on October 30, 2026.

There are at least a million businesses using the company's AI agents in WhatsApp and Messenger, to say nothing of other services like Instagram, Facebook, its widely used advertising service, or its less widely used business suite. As noted by Nieman Lab, almost every news publisher has at least one Meta business account.

Meta defines business customers as those "using ads or marketing messages, selling or listing products, developing apps, creating or using a product catalog, managing a Page, managing a Group for business purposes, using any business product, such as Ads Manager or Meta Business Suite."

The added language grants Meta the right to use automated software with created credentials to scrape customer content and use it for the enhancement of its products, including AI models.

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users' use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs.

Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.

Danielle Coffey, president and CEO of the News/Media Alliance, condemned Meta's move.

"Meta’s new commercial terms of use are outrageous and probably illegal," she said in a statement . "The company’s decision to withhold access to its audience unless businesses allow Meta to scrape content from their websites is an appalling, bad-faith policy, and a clear abuse of the company’s market power. It cannot be allowed to be implemented on October 30."

Coffey said any business with intellectual property and a Meta account should question what these terms allow.

Eric Goldman, associate dean for research and professor of law at Santa Clara University School of Law, told The Register in an interview that Meta's revised terms of service raise both procedural and substantive issues.

While it's already commonplace for businesses to change their contractual terms after customers sign up, he said, applying these changes to customers who already have a multifaceted relationship with Meta can be challenging.

"When I talk to my students about how to amend [terms of service agreements], I say that you have to give users a bona fide option to reject the terms," he explained. "Otherwise it's just Hobson's choice or Morton's fork ."

For example, he said, if Meta's business customers have prepaid for anything, is the only option to avoid these terms to end the business relationship, and if so, is Meta prepared to refund the prepaid fees?

The procedural issue, he said, is what this does to existing business relationships and how it can be properly enforced as a change to existing terms.

Then in terms of the substance of the change, Goldman said that, while he's inclined to assume those drafting contracts do so in good faith, "Meta has no reservoir of good faith among the community that it can draw upon."

Meta's history of sacrificing user privacy and mental health, as documented in the Cambridge Analytica scandal and the social media addiction settlement with 52 state attorneys general, drained that reservoir in the course of the company's 22-year history of data harvesting.

Goldman said that it's easy to assume the worst possible interpretation of Meta's contractual language because the company has "disrespected our trust so often."

He added that while news reports have indicated that Meta intends to allow businesses to signal their crawling preferences through robots.txt directives, that's not spelled out.

"That all sounds great, but the language doesn't expressly say that Meta will respect those robots.txt instructions," he said. "The law doesn't necessarily compel anyone to respect robots.txt files. And now we're back to the good faith/bad faith scenario."

Goldman said there have been past terms of service controversies , like GeoCities in 1999 and Instagram in 2012, that haven't led to disaster.

"The drafters [in those instances] had some particular problem they were trying to solve, but in drafting around that problem may not have been careful enough to avoid grabbing rights that really set people off," he said. "This looks a lot like that to me. But again, that's actually giving Meta the presumption of good faith. And I just can't do that anymore."

Meta did not respond to a request for comment.®

item.title: Ubuntu Stonking Stingray swims into spotlight with pre-release kernel
item.description:
The latest interim release of Ubuntu is here, complete with kernel 7.3 – even though it isn't officially out yet. It also includes a new speech-to-text system that is intriguing but not fully useful.

Ubuntu 26.10 "Stonking Stingray" arrived on time. This is just a couple of weeks after the beta version that we looked at earlier this month , suggesting that the team didn’t encounter any show-stopper bugs.

The faster kernel release cycle that Canonical adopted in 2024 has slightly bitten them this time around: the Linux kernel’s new faster AI-boosted release cycle means that 7.2 is relatively old now, but 7.3 isn’t quite ready yet; at the time of writing, it’s on Release Candidate 7 – but Canonical has jumped the gun and used it anyway. So, the release version of Ubuntu 26.10 comes with a pre-release kernel, and machines will get updated to the completed 7.3 as soon as it’s available.

We tried the default GNOME edition, with GNOME 51. It looks identical to the beta version. The most visible difference in this release is in the window-tiling assistant, which now displays a Windows-like transient pop-up box offering various tiled arrangements when you drag a window to the edge of the screen.

The Myna speech-to-text tool, whose announcement we covered back in June , is now available – albeit as a technology preview. We tested the beta on an old ThinkPad, and while the pre-release OS ran perfectly, Myna didn't work. (Incidentally, after switching to a non-GPU LLM, it does work in the release version – just very slowly.)

So, we tried the release version on our newer testbed machine, a Dell XPS 9370. The installation process is more straightforward now, with some official instructions , and as the Dell doesn't have an unsupported Nvidia GPU to complicate things, it worked fine. The installation pulls in nearly a gigabyte of dependencies and language model files: since the installation ISO is already 6⅔ GB, it's probably a good thing that it’s not included.

We tested it in the Writer module of LibreOffice 26.8. Invoking it is as simple as pressing Super+J , and then talking. Using the laptop’s built-in microphone, accuracy was poor, but with a USB headset, it improved markedly. It’s a little odd to watch as the model revises the text as you go along, going back and altering words as later ones resolve ambiguities, but it did the job.

It doesn’t understand punctuation or commands: words such as "comma," "full stop," "new line," "delete," and so on, were entered into the document along with other text. For a preview, though, it's impressive, and for those who have problems with the use of their arms – such as the Reg FOSS desk just three years ago – this is a seriously useful extra. Ubuntu now just has to catch up with macOS and Windows, both of which have offered speech input for several years – but it's finally entered the race. This is one use of LLMs of which we heartily approve.

Alongside the flagship GNOME edition, all the flavors have been updated, which hasn't happened for about a year. For some flavors, this means new versions of their respective desktops, depending on the release cycle of the respective environment. As we said when we looked at the beta release, Kubuntu 26.10 comes with KDE Plasma 6.7.5, which is the final Plasma release to support X11.

Although Ubuntu MATE skipped the LTS release earlier this year, it's back with the Stonking release: Ubuntu MATE 26.10 will come as good news for fans of this retro GNOME 2 style desktop.

A year ago, Ubuntu Unity missed the 25.10 release, and 26.04 is not an LTS, so fans of Canonical's in-house desktop should take a close look at Ubuntu Unity 26.10 . A visible change from previous releases is that it's picked up some accessory apps from the Lomiri desktop , which is the community continuation of what was going to be Unity 8. Ubuntu Unity 26.10 uses the Lomiri terminal emulator by default, and Lomiri's File Manager is available as an alternative to the default Nemo file manager. The "minimal" installation of this release is even more stripped back than Xubuntu Minimal – this version doesn't have the Snap subsystem installed at all.

Ubuntu Budgie 26.10 has the very latest Budgie desktop version 10.10.3 , which brings some accessibility improvements. Ubuntu Cinnamon 26.10 has an updated version of Mint’s Cinnamon environment, too – it includes the very latest Cinnamon 6.6.9, released in June. Lubuntu 26.10 includes the latest LXQt 2.4 , which arrived too close to the release of Lubuntu 26.04 to be incorporated.

The other 26.10 flavors are more modest releases, which just pick up the latest versions of their components. Under the hood, there are some deeper changes that affect all editions. As we mentioned in the beta version, more core CLI tools have been replaced with new Rust versions, now including the NTP-sync daemon. Stonking replaces dbus-daemon with dbus-broker , and it uses systemd 261.3. The server version has been updated as well, and now includes AMD ROCm 10.0 , OpenSSL 4, OpenSSH 10.5, and the Rust upki tool for revoking security certificates.

Canonical’s home-grown TPM-backed full disk encryption is present, but intrepid experimenters who have enabled that on 26.04 can't upgrade for now – this should follow later.

One of the benefits of increasingly mature FOSS desktops is that upgrades are increasingly routine, so long as you haven't rolled up your sleeves, lifted the hood, and started customizing the OS. If you just install packages from Snapcraft and leave the OS alone, interim versions are pretty safe these days, and so is the upgrade process. It's one way to avoid being nagged about Ubuntu Pro, if that irks you. Pro is not available on interim releases. By default, LTS versions don't automatically offer to upgrade to interim ones – if you want it, you must opt in . We suggest leaving it until the final version of the kernel, but otherwise, it’s already in good shape. ®

item.title: New online tool will check lawyers' sloppy AI-written briefs since they can't seem to be bothered
item.description:
For lawyers who love to use AI to write legal briefs, there's just one problem: bots hallucinate and make things up. Fortunately, a new tool, CiteProof , promises to crawl over briefs and filings for fabricated case citations and misquoted court opinions before they result in sanctions, fines, or just plain embarrassing dressing downs from a judge.

This is hardly a new problem, with lawyers relying on AI to do their work for several years with predictably horrible results. Even if GPT-4 was capable of passing a bar exam in 2023, that doesn’t mean it wasn’t hallucinating case law .

OpenAI models aren’t alone in getting lawyers in trouble, either - Claude was actually thrown under the bus by Anthropic’s own lawyers last year when defending the company from a music publishing copyright lawsuit. A declaration in the case from an Anthropic data scientist contained a pair of Claude-formatted citations that pointed to improper records, and lawyers didn’t catch it in review. The lawyers blamed Claude for the issue.

Stories of AI hallucinations winding up in legal briefs are everywhere nowadays, and have had serious consequences beyond professional rebukes: A Georgia court decision was even vacated last year after a court order was found to contain fictional citations.

In short, AI and the legal world, which demands precision and accuracy, don’t always mix , so a fact checker that can do a better job than apparently absent-minded human reviewers is needed. CiteProof wants to be that fact checker.

Free users can run individual checks through CiteProof to look for citations or statutes, while paid users can run in-depth scans that include more detailed verification reports, quotation checking, bulk scanning, and the like.

CiteProof admitted that, as a small operation, some vibe-coding was involved in the creation of the platform, but no AI is involved in checking legal briefs for AI.

“You cannot reliably catch AI hallucinations with more AI guesswork,” a CiteProof spokesperson told us. “This is the foundational principle of CiteProof.”

There aren’t any LLMs or probabilistic models under CiteProof’s hood, we’re told, with queries instead relying on direct, deterministic searches of public court records to look for evidence that what AI is citing for lawyers isn’t being completely made up.

It’s not going to tell you whether you’re making a good argument, mind you - CiteProof is just going to free up that legal assistant to do something more productive than checking citations.

The only thing that leaves CiteProof’s servers, the company claims, is strings extracted from citations that can be input into CourtListener to figure out if they’re real. Everything runs in the US, and nothing is stored or transmitted to an LLM at any point, CiteProof says.

But why encourage lawyers to use more AI if it’s not a reliable tool for their purposes? The genie is already out of the bottle, CiteProof says, even if it is a real messy genie who just makes stuff up.

“Lawyers and associates are already using AI to speed up research and drafting, and that adoption isn't stopping,” the representative told us. “CiteProof isn't encouraging blind AI adoption—it acts as an objective, non-AI guardrail to ensure that if someone uses generative tools to draft, fabricated citations are caught before hitting a court docket.”

It’s better than nothing, even if it doesn’t come cheap: A single brief costs $49 to check if you don’t opt for the limited free tier, with bundles offering multiple briefs at a discount ($199 for a five-pack), all the way up to $499 a month for 200 brief reviews for law firms that just can’t stop relying on AI to make their arguments for them. ®

item.title: Just How Rosy Is That Datacenter Buildout Forecast?
item.description:
No matter how much money anyone throws at it, the GenAI boom can only continue to grow as fast as datacenters are built and powered up to accept machinery.

No amount of political, social, or economic pressure can speed up how power generation equipment is installed at datacenters or at utilities. No one was expecting this AI boom to skyrocket so, and supply chains from chip manufacturing equipment to chip makers to those who make all of the equipment that goes into power distribution in the electric grids and within the datacenters were not ready to ramp as quickly as the industry seems to require.

For now at least, it takes people to build all of these datacenters and indeed anything else we want to provide shelter for ourselves, our businesses, and our public facilities. And it is convenient, perhaps, that there are high interest rates for mortgages at a time when datacenter builders want more people working on their projects instead of building homes or offices. (Yes, people still go to the office, and thankfully I have not had to do that since 1996.)

Jason Furman , an economics professor at Harvard University, posted this neat chart on X that shows the growth rates of construction projects thus far in 2026 up through August:

This is yet another data point that shows just how much datacenter construction and power utility construction are helping to prop up the economy in the United States. And just to be clear, this data from the US Census Bureau and the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, and it includes the cost of construction materials and the labor on construction projects. It explicitly does not include any compute, storage, or networking gear inside of those datacenters, but it does include the cost of power distribution and energy backup equipment in datacenter facilities.

As you can see, datacenter capacity construction increases, and to a certain extent for power utilities as well, are counter-balancing the declines seen in commercial and residential construction in the United States.

It is tough to get a sense of the spending levels for datacenters from this chart, and so we poked around and found a monthly chart that runs from January 2014 through August 2026 from the US Census Bureau, which was put together by the Our World In Data project at Oxford University. Take a look:

This chart is based on inflation-adjusted spending pegged to 2021 US dollars.

You can really see how the GenAI boom, which is driving datacenter construction spending increases in the United States, started in November 2022. Since that time, we are in a very different market – up and to the right, and accelerating.

This data from the Census Bureau does not include datacenter spending by federal, state, or local governments, buy the way. Not that this is very large compared to what the hyperscalers, cloud builders, and AI model builders are ponying up. Government datacenter spending would be a tiny part of the signal that would not change its shape by much.

Which brings me to a very detailed and interesting forecast of datacenter spending that the analysts at Jeffries put together with the help of Aterio , a market researcher specialized in datacenter forecasts among many other sectors.

Aterio provided the historical context, and Jonathan Petersen, managing director at Jeffries, put together a base forecast with a bull and a bear variant to that base case to bracket what they expect datacenter spending to be from 2026 through 2030. Here’s the table that gives you the data:

And for those of you who also like to look at data visually, here is the companion chart:

Our thanks to Petersen for permission to share this data with you.

“The AI industry has a datacenter problem,” Petersen writes in a report released on October 9. “Demand for inference and frontier model training is growing faster than developers can bring capacity online. Our dataset tracks ~65 IT GW of DCs under construction (~140 percent of installed capacity), and another ~361 GW of future announced projects (~760 percent). However, it will take time to bring that capacity online, and many projects will be delayed or canceled. We expect 12.9 GWs of new capacity in 2026 and 18 GWs in 2027.”

This model only predicts installed gigawatts in North America for IT gear, not the cost of building those datacenters or putting the gear inside them to make them useful or the power and cooling costs that enliven the facilities and gear. This model does not just take the forecasts by datacenter operators and businesses that run their own datacenters at face value, but looks at the probability that projects will be completed, and to what extend based on intentions.

To say the least, Jeffries is appropriately cynical about how the datacenter buildout will pan out, given the constraints on all of the supply inputs and labor to build datacenters.

“The ability to bring new datacenter capacity online is often reduced to a discussion measuring new grid interconnects or behind-the-meter power generation as primary gating factors,” says Petersen. “Or tracking hyperscaler capex and assuming that spending more capex will create new data centers. Or, measuring chip sales projections from the semiconductor industry. But any of those discussions in isolation misses the bigger picture: it takes all of those inputs, plus available labor, manufacturing of electrical and cooling equipment, and a cooperative political and regulatory environment to move a data center project from the pipeline to online capacity.”

The labor shortage and the increasing political pressure for datacenters to pay their fair share of the cost of electricity generation and a rising skepticism about the financial benefits to the communities that host datacenters is what is driving the bear case. The bull case is more about supply chain issues for datacenter construction easing somewhat, but not enough for everything desired and planned to be built. This latter point is the point . Even the bull case assumes lots of delays and some cancellations.

To show you the gap between planned capacity and the estimates by Jeffries, even the hyperscalers, who have tons of money and very strong balance sheets, are not going to be able to build at the rate they want. The planned and estimated North American hyperscaler datacenter capacity for 2026 is 6.21 gigawatts in 2026. (The year is pretty much done, so this convergence makes sense.) For 2027, the hyperscalers in North America are talking about wanting to do 8.37 gigawatts of datacenter buildout, but Jeffries thinks only 7.53 gigawatts will get built for these companies. In 2028, the aspirations are huge, and the built capacity Jeffries expects will be lower, not higher, with hyperscalers planning for 10.13 gigawatts of buildout and Petersen and crew expecting only 6.54 gigawatts to be completed. The 2029 plans are for just under 18 gigawatts among the hyperscalers in North America, but Jeffries thinks only 5.86 gigawatts will get done. And in 2030, the aspirations will shrink to 13.82 gigawatts for the hyperscaler facilities in the United States and Canada and the expected build will look more like 4.46 gigawatts.

These are huge gaps. In 2026, labor is the biggest damper on datacenter spending, and in 2027 through 2029, it will be cooling equipment. In 2030, the main constraint will be available power, says Jeffries. All of these constraints are always present, of course.

item.title: Networking problems after the October 2026 Windows update? NTLM might be to blame
item.description:
The October 2026 Windows security update may break networking for some customers who are still clinging to long-deprecated NTLMv1 security.

A seemingly minor change in the update could have major implications for administrators and enterprises that haven't fully moved away from the legacy technology.

Before the October 2026 update, Windows permitted NTLMv1-derived credentials for Single Sign-On and generated warning events. After the update, requests to use NTLMv1-derived credentials are blocked.

It comes down to the BlockNtlmSSO registry value. If it hasn't been set, Windows will now use Enforce mode (1) instead of Audit mode (0), thus blocking requests and potentially impacting Wi-Fi, Ethernet, and VPN authentication, and therefore connections.

The update does not set the value of BlockNtlmSSO , and administrators can set it to 0 to temporarily allow NTLMv1-derived Single Sign-On credentials. However, Microsoft noted, "Using Audit mode reduces the protection provided by Enforce mode and should only be considered as a scoped, temporary security exception."

To be clear, this is not a bug and is by design. The addition of NTLM to the deprecation list occurred in 2024 , and Microsoft added audit logs for NTLMv1 usage in late August 2025. The Windows giant has made no secret of its desire to ditch the legacy technology, stating in 2023 , "Our end goal is eliminating the need to use NTLM at all."

The problem is NTLM's longevity. It appeared in 1993 with Windows NT 3.1, and removing it from enterprise environments has proven tricky, even though it is somewhat insecure by modern standards. Microsoft removed it from Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025, but some remnants can still be found, notably when using MS-CHAPv2-based connections, including PEAP-MSCHAPv2, and EAP-MSCHAPv2, in a domain-joined environment.

Hence the introduction of the audit mode in 2025, to help administrators spot where the technology was still being used.

It is now 2026, and Microsoft has taken the next step. If Credential Guard is not enabled and BlockNtlmSSO is not set to Audit mode (0), the use of NTLMv1-derived credentials will be blocked as Microsoft works "to finalize the disablement of NTLMv1."

There is no indication of how long the BlockNtlmSSO workaround (setting the value to Audit mode) will work - most likely until the next major Windows release. In September, Microsoft said , "In-market versions of Windows client and Windows Server will continue to support NTLM." However, it also stated, "Our long-term objective is a Windows platform that doesn't need NTLM at all."

As such, if the message wasn't already clear, the move to enforce it by default makes it impossible to miss. The technology still exists in the operating system, but it is on its way out and will be removed in a future Windows release.

Problems with networking after the October 2026 Windows security update could therefore signal that migration plans are not as far along, or as complete, as administrators might have thought. ®

item.title: SPONSORED: Global Data Centers weighs the price tag of not building fast enough
item.description:
The next 200-megawatt data center permitted in your county probably won't look like the buildings you remember from a decade ago. It will occupy the footprint of two or three football fields and draw more power than most nearby industrial parks combined. It will also likely trigger a town hall meeting before the first pad is poured. That collision between AI-driven demand and physical reality is what NTT Global Data Centers set out to quantify in its new AI Stress Test Report .

The report models three growth trajectories through 2030 and stress-tests each against the constraints operators hit, such as land availability, water consumption, specialized labor and more. The middle (baseline) scenario projects annual demand growth of about 23 percent, which pencils out to roughly $3.8 trillion of additional investment in digital infrastructure. Ramp to the accelerated case and the figure climbs to $5.7 trillion.

Bruno Berti, CTO at NTT Global Data Centers, notes that he has watched the size envelope stretch beyond recognition.

"We used to build ten-megawatt buildings, smaller buildings, to support some of these applications," says Berti. "But now we're building buildings that are hundreds of megawatts, double the size, sizes of two, maybe sometimes three football fields."

Why permitting became the choke point

Ask most operators what will bottleneck AI infrastructure and you'll hear GPUs, transformers, switchgear. NTT Global Data Centers’ stress test suggests something more mundane: paperwork, planning and process. Power availability and deployment timelines, not fiber capacity, are the gating factors in the scenarios modeled. Berti puts it plainly: it doesn't matter how quickly you can get GPUs if you can't get a permit to put them anywhere.

That reframes the strategy question. Berti argues against a "build, baby, build" reflex, preferring a portfolio approach that treats capacity expansion as a system-wide coordination problem rather than a land race.

The misconceptions that stall projects

Two objections come up in almost every community consultation, according to Berti: data centers waste water, and they steal power from the grid. Both are misconceptions and come from an older generation of facilities. Modern designs, he says, use liquid cooling technology, which removes heat more effectively, eliminating excess water waste. Additionally, operators plan the new class of hundred-megawatt-plus sites in partnership with utilities years in advance, often with on-site solar, wind or other renewable generation that can help stabilize the grid rather than drain it.

His conclusion is blunt: transparency builds trust. So, the industry has to stop treating what it does as a secret and start to build that trust through education and partnership if it wants the permits it will need through the decade to turn capacity into reliable AI infrastructure that can benefit communities, policymakers and businesses alike.

Sponsored by NTT Global Data Centers.

item.title: Uncle Scam Wants You … to cough up your cash and personal data, FBI warns ahead of midterms
item.description:
The FBI is once again warning US citizens to be on the lookout for the scams that are so often rife around election season.

With November’s midterms fast approaching, the FBI said scammers are known to use the names, imagery, and slogans of high-profile candidates for a range of frauds.

These are often related to making donations and selling merchandise, but can also be geared toward stealing personal data for use in follow-on scams.

And of course, more recently, fraudsters’ efforts can be all the more convincing given the rise in AI use and deepfake technology, which can also be used to more accurately imitate the likenesses of candidates and other officials.

Campaign investment pool schemes are among the four big frauds the FBI wants the public to watch out for over the next few weeks.

These involve scammers convincing their marks to pay into a campaign pool, which ostensibly pays out to all of those who donated after the candidate wins.

More commonly, these types of pooled investment scams are based on collective investments into stocks and other appreciating assets.

The FBI did not provide details about these campaign pools’ investment incentives or how victims are supposedly able to increase their stake by donating to the cause, but did say that no genuine campaign donations appreciate over time.

Another common donation-based scam to be wary of is the one that convinces victims to fund a fake political action committee (PAC), one that collects supporters’ cash and promises to hand it to their favored party or candidate.

Instead of forwarding money to a specific political campaign, however, the scammers pocket it all for themselves.

Fraudsters are also known for claiming to sell merchandise related to political campaigns – orders that ultimately go unfulfilled.

These constitute non-delivery scams, which rank in the top five genres of internet cons, according to the Internet Crime Complaint Center’s (IC3) most recent annual report .

The same report put phishing at the number one spot in that same list, and the classic cyberattack features on the FBI’s list of midterm-related scams, too.

Creating a sense of urgency, scammers will text victims claiming they have not yet registered to vote, and asking them to follow a link to a webpage where they can enter their details and complete the process, which of course leads to identity theft.

While the FBI doesn’t include this detail in its advisory, Texans should be especially wary of these communication attempts given the recent computer issues that led to a massive backlog in registration applications.

As of September 22, 226, around 600,000 applications were allegedly in limbo after a website flaw failed to record voters’ intentions to vote, and therefore did not receive registration forms from the Texas Secretary of State (SOS), according to a lawsuit [PDF] filed by voter registration organizations last week.

However, spokesperson for the SOS’ office Alicia Pierce told USA Today that the backlog was only in the tens of thousands and that as of this week it was all-clear.

Scammers may nevertheless continue to capitalize on the public awareness of the backlog when devising the lures for their phishing campaigns.

The feds advised the public to be wary of these kinds of communications, and verify all political organizations, such as PACs, via the government’s election commission website.

Although some scam PACs can appear on the website as registered, you can usually discern the suspicious ones when they report high expenses for matters such as consulting, fundraising, and other admin costs.

The FBI's advisory follows separate action taken by X, which on Wednesday evening warned that influence campaigns originating from Iran, Russia, and China were targeting US voters, amplifying content across the political spectrum.

The social media platform responded by nuking more than 13,000 accounts linked to the foreign interference attempts. ®

item.title: Attack on BAE-managed system disrupts US bankruptcy courts
item.description:
The US' bankruptcy courts are currently down owing to what officials are calling a “cybersecurity incident.”

The Administrative Office of the US Courts said the websites and systems that support the Bankruptcy Noticing Center (BNC), which manages electronic comms related to bankruptcy cases, were pulled offline while the vendor investigates.

UK-based BAE Systems runs the affected systems and websites on behalf of the Federal Judiciary, and is “working to restore operations,” according to an announcement by the US Courts on Thursday.

“As a result of the incident, all access to the BNC systems and websites that BAE operates on behalf of the judiciary and the related bankruptcy noticing process are unavailable at this time, including bnc.uscourts.gov, bankruptcynotices.uscourts.gov, notices.uscourts.gov, and the National Creditor Registration Service," it said.

“The incident has also halted the BNC’s production and distribution of bankruptcy notices for bankruptcy courts.”

While the public notice was published on Thursday, the issues affecting the BNC systems began a few days earlier, on October 9, according to the Bankruptcy Court of the Eastern District of Texas.

Alongside its own announcement , the same court published a general order indicating that for any case filed on or after September 14 with an active motion to stay, that delay would be extended by an additional 30 days.

The court said it will continue to accept filings, open cases, and process documents, but said there may be a delay in the entry and service of notices and orders until the issues are resolved.

The courts' ability to process electronic and paper bankruptcy notices is affected, and it applies to federal bankruptcy courts across the country.

BAE Systems did not immediately respond to requests for more information.

The disruption comes at a difficult time for the US public sector, which has struggled with multiple recent cyberattacks.

ShinyHunters' attack on the FBI in September is doubtless the most high-profile of these, although the Arizona Judicial Branch confirmed an attack on the state’s court systems at around the same time.

Officials said the “criminal hackers or their bots” were responsible for stealing personal data and backup court files.

The US Courts also said in August 2025 that it was stepping up its cybersecurity measures in response to increased targeting of its case management system . ®

item.title: British watchdog seeks tougher terms around Microsoft's dominance of business software
item.description:
The UK's competition watchdog wants to designate Microsoft with strategic market status (SMS) in business software, allowing the regulator it to intervene to level the playing field, and says it is considering other areas for investigation.

Regulators around the world are watching to see what the UK decides in this case, with bodies such as the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and the European Commission mulling similar actions.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is opening a consultation on whether to tag the Redmond software giant with strategic market status in respect of its portfolio of business software applications.

This follows an investigation the regulator started back in May into Microsoft’s software portfolio including Word, Excel, Outlook, PowerPoint and Teams, plus its security, server and operating systems. The watchdog is also probing whether Microsoft enjoys a position of “substantial and entrenched market power” through the suite of software that could be seen as stifling competition and harming buyer choice.

It lays out its proposed decision in a document [PDF] and is inviting comments that must be submitted by November 13. The CMA will make its final decision by February 13, 2027.

Bargain spotter

The CMA makes it clear the company holds a strong position in each of the five areas it investigated (personal computer operating systems, productivity software suites, security software, server operating systems and relational database management systems), and that customers face barriers when switching providers – limiting their choice and weakening the ability of other software developers to offer rival products.

Its proposal document notes Microsoft has been by far the largest provider of business software in the UK for decades. It finds that many customers view Microsoft's portfolio as a unified software environment, forming an end-to-end, integrated stack which makes for easier technical integration between products, with discounted pricing for buying whole bundles of applications together.

This makes customers less likely to adopt products from alternative providers that may offer similar or superior functionality, as doing so would duplicate licensing costs for products already in their Microsoft bundle, the CMA says.

“Organizations should be able to choose the products that work best for them, switch provider when they want to and combine services from different suppliers. We want to ensure businesses have the freedom to choose how they use Microsoft’s products alongside alternatives,” said CMA chief exec Sarah Cardell.

Finding that the criteria for SMS designation are met would not imply or assume wrongdoing on Microsoft’s part, the regulator stresses.

A separate document [PDF] spells out the potential interventions that the CMA could make. These include ensuring that Microsoft’s technical design choices do not restrict the ability to use other providers; that commercial arrangements (like bundling) do not limit effective competition; and preventing Microsoft from using its market power in business software to distort competition in adjacent activities, such as cloud services.


Rivals back licensing scrutiny
